title: Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says
description: The co-pilot who attempted to take control of a Flydubai plane travelling to Israel attacked the pilot with a crash axe, the United Arab Emirates pros
body: The co-pilot who attempted to take control of a Flydubai plane travelling to Israel attacked the pilot with a crash axe, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv carrying more than 170 people plunged 17,000ft (5,200m) two and a half hours into its journey, before passengers managed to overpower the attacker and successfully take control of the plane.Capt Smit Machchhar said he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in.Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.A crash axe is usually kept ​in the cockpit in case of emergencies.The weapon used has been a key question for investigators, given the stringent security on such a sensitive route. Early reports from passengers on board had suggested it might have been a knife.The UAE attorney general told state media that investigations were ongoing to determine the full circumstances and motives of the incident.The co-pilot who launched the attack was an Omani national, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Multiple media outlets including Reuters, CNN and The New York Times have named him as Hamam al-Hammami. There has been no official confirmation of this.While working at another airline, Oman Air, US media reported that Al-Hammami was removed from flight training because of concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at Oman's national airline.He completed a three-year distance-learning course at Buckinghamshire New University in the UK and graduated with a degree in aviation management in 2023, the university said. It added he did not take any pilot training at the school.Speaking to Fox News, Netanyahu said that after the attacker was subdued on the flight, he called out to the crew "Kill me, kill me!"The Israeli prime minister added: "So, it's clear that he was suicidal… It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane."He also said the attacker "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination".The UAE's attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said investigations into the incident revealed that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act", according to the country's state news agency.He also said investigations were under way to establish the circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident.Machchhar, who was stabbed in the attack, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.The pilot, who is from India, was in "good health and recovering well", the Indian embassy in the UAE said on Thursday."I am confident that the recovery will be there and I will become fit and healthy again," Machchhar said.About two and half hours after the plane took off from Dubai International Airport it begun to plunge sharply. The plane signalled a "general emergency" code, squawk 7700, before switching to squawk 7500, a code reporting "unlawful interference", or hijacking.In an interview with the BBC, one passenger described the moment he realised that something was wrong.Almog Itali said: "Suddenly the aeroplane started to, like a rollercoaster, to drop down [with] a massive G-force. It was falling down for 20 or 30 seconds, rapidly, and then balanced, and then started once again to fall down."People then began to rush to the cockpit, he said.Israeli President Isaac Herzog said on Thursday that the alarm was raised onboard by an Israeli woman, Tali Manes, who heard a commotion coming from the cockpit. Her husband, Zvika, along with three other men - Yaniv Hayun, Dr Shota Musayev and Asaf Rajuan - entered the cockpit after Capt Machchhar managed to open the door despite his injuries. Hayun said, in a video released by the prime minister's office, that the attacker was "trying to destroy the instruments in order to disable the plane".Hayun then described putting the attacker in a chokehold and pulling him outside the cockpit before other passengers helped to pin him down.He added that he "pulled the controls" of the plane. "The plane started to level out, a bit more, and then [another] pilot told me he was taking control from there," he said.In an interview with CNN on Wednesday evening, Netanyahu said the stabbed pilot, passengers and second crew had "managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster".

schema.headline: Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says

title: UK-Iranian dual national arrested over RAF Fairford investigation bailed
description: A UK-Iranian dual national arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with an incident at RAF Fairford has been released on
body: A UK-Iranian dual national arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with an incident at RAF Fairford has been released on bail.The 25-year-old man was arrested in the London borough of Westminster on Thursday. Searches of two properties in the same area have now finished. A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase in Gloucestershire last weekend.Five other men in their twenties were arrested and were subsequently released on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London.The investigation into the circumstances surrounding the events are continuing, police said.Last weekend, the five men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident.The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles.They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a Cobra meeting that afternoon in response. He later said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident, but did not provide any more details.Tehran has strongly denied any involvement. The Iranian embassy in London said on Monday that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".Late on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a TV show that it was clear a "foreign actor" had been involved in events over the weekend.Without providing evidence or giving further details, he told Fox News network's "Hannity" programme: "What happened, what almost happened, what could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It's one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor."Speaking earlier at the Oval Office, US President Donald Trump said he would not have let the five men arrested out on bail, and that he was "surprised" they had been released."We know everything about them, we would not have released them," he said, adding that the UK had worked with the US "very closely" on this.

schema.headline: UK-Iranian dual national arrested over RAF Fairford investigation bailed

title: Tories pledge to build 50,000 new prison places
description: The Conservatives have promised to build 50,000 new prison places in England and Wales to stop criminals being released early, if they return to gover
body: The Conservatives have promised to build 50,000 new prison places in England and Wales to stop criminals being released early, if they return to government.The party said it would cost £2bn per year to build and run the new prisons, funded by spending cuts including to the foreign aid budget.On Thursday hundreds of prisoners were released early, under new rules introduced to prevent jails reaching capacity, with around 4,500 due to be freed by next summer.Labour blamed the previous Tory government for leaving "our criminal justice system at breaking point" and said the party's proposals were not "credible".The announcement comes as Conservative members gather for the party's annual conference in Birmingham, which begins on Sunday.Prisons in England and Wales have been running close to capacity for years, with the latest government figures showing they are 98% full.Under the latest early release scheme, eligible prisoners can now be released on a community licence after serving one-third of their jail sentence.Those excluded include prisoners convicted of murder, manslaughter, a sexual or grooming-related offence, or a driving offence that led to a death.The government has also effectively scrapped one-year jail terms.The Tories said they would use extra prison capacity to reverse these measures.An early release programme introduced by the previous Conservative government saw more than 10,000 prisoners freed early between October 2023 and September 2024.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "A violent criminal doesn't become less dangerous just because the government has run out of prison cells."She added: "[Labour's] answer is to let dangerous offenders out even earlier instead of building the prison spaces we need."Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said: "The Tories are taking the public for fools. Across 14 years in government, they added just 500 prison places and closed 23 prisons. "Now Kemi Badenoch expects the British people to believe they'll build 50,000."The Liberal Democrats also criticised the Tory plan, describing it as "fantasy numbers funded by breaking promises"."Much like their economic plans, something doesn't add up," added the party's justice spokesperson Jess Brown-Fuller. Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy told BBC Breakfast the 50,000 extra places would be built within six to seven years "and the vast majority of them will be built in the first parliament".Meanwhile, the Prison Governors' Association said "long-term investment" was needed and warned a "staffing crisis" would pose challenges to delivering new prisons.If the party wins power, the Tories said they would introduce legislation early in the new Parliament to override planning and procurement barriers, allowing the process to be "fast-tracked".It said the use of private finance would help speed up delivery and control costs.There are currently around 89,000 useable prison places in England and Wales, according to the latest government figures.The Tories said their proposals would increase this figure by more than 50%, with the vast majority of new places expected within the party's first Parliament in government - up to five years - and the full increase delivered within seven years.The £2bn a year cost would be funded through savings in other areas, including cutting the aid budget by £1bn and reducing the budget of the Department for Culture Media and Sport by £1bn.The Labour government has promised to add 14,000 extra prison space by 2031.The Tories argued increasing prison places would cut crime and prevent reoffending by keeping serious criminals off the streets.Timothy said: "Prison works. It works by punishing and deterring, but most importantly by incapacitating. "Prison should keep violent and repeat offenders away from the law-abiding public."The prison population has risen significantly in recent decades, partly as a result of longer sentences and more people being returned to prison for breaching the conditions of their release. Successive governments have pledged to increase the number of prison places - but delivery has often fallen short of those promises.New prisons take years to build, often facing local opposition and obstacles in the planning process.The Prison Governors' Association said: "Building 50,000 cells is one thing; finding the thousands of experienced officers, governors and specialists needed to run them safely is quite another."Politicians have spent years announcing prison places while the service struggles with overcrowding, ageing infrastructure and staffing shortages. The real test is not how many places can be promised, but how many prisons can be operated safely, effectively, and sustainably."

schema.headline: Tories pledge to build 50,000 new prison places

title: Spoilers: Is social media ruining gig surprises?
description: Spoiler alert! Is social media ruining big gig surprises? Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Big moments from Olivia Rodrigo's tour were dissect
body: Spoiler alert! Is social media ruining big gig surprises? Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Big moments from Olivia Rodrigo's tour were dissected online shortly after her opening night BySrosh Khan and Riyah CollinsBBC NewsbeatMonths before you have a chance to see your favourite artist, chances are you already know some of the big moments they have planned.  You'll also probably know the set list, the stage design, and - if you've really been paying attention - where to stand to get the best view. When it comes to films and TV series, spoilers tend to be guarded against with warnings.But for many major gigs, there's no escaping a stream of fan videos from the shows if you're online, whether you like it or not.Last week, US pop star Olivia Rodrigo kicked off her Unraveled tour, and surprises from the show, which scores of fans have paid a lot of money to see, have already been dissected online.Tours by Harry Styles, Charli XCX and Ariana Grande have also been filmed from every angle and shared over the past few months.While some fans lap up the opportunity to see what's coming, others are taking extreme measures to preserve the element of surprise. Image source, HandoutImage caption, Aurélia Collins always aims to go to gigs not knowing what to expectAurélia Collins is one of them, spending weeks trying to trick her algorithm into not serving her content about her favourite artists and tapping "not interested" when videos come up, even though she says "it hurts my soul". It can mean her social media feed is a bit bland, but she tells BBC Newsbeat "it's worth it for the surprise".The 20-year-old criminology student is a huge One Direction fan and says she just about managed to avoid spoilers for Styles' Together, Together tour over summer. But when one slipped through the net about Niall Horan before she was able to see his show in London on Saturday - her first time seeing him live after being a fan for 16 years - she was "gutted"."When I was younger, we couldn't afford to go to events like this and hear live music and because it's such a moment, I really want to take it in," she says."I want the full experience, and that includes the element of surprise that people that go to the opening night of the tour can get."Image source, HandoutImage caption, Georgia McAdam says videos online help her plan her gig experience Not all fans think spoilers are a bad thing, though. In fact, Georgia McAdam claims she loves them."I'm the type of person that loves to be prepared," the 22-year-old says. "I love to know what the stage is looking like, what the set list consists of and where to stand."McAdam's a huge Olivia Rodrigo fan and sees online spoilers more as "teasers". She feels no amount of online videos can ever really take away from the excitement of the real thing. "Sometimes you get different surprise songs to what's online or you never know what an artist might do," she adds.'You have to not look at TikTok'Some artists have reacted by switching up their sets in small ways each night to make sure fans coming to later dates still see something unexpected. Taylor Swift had bespoke outfits and surprise songs during her mammoth Eras tour, Sabrina Carpenter performed unique positions during her song Juno and switched up her Nonsense outro, and Jay-Z has been changing up his set list on his current run.But the Guardian's deputy music editor Laura Snapes says it's not just fans who can benefit from these twists. "One way that they can make sure they're staying in the press is by having something different happen in their show every night," Snapes says. "Obviously, it'll be all over TikTok."Figures shared by TikTok with Newsbeat show posts using #CharliXCX have increased by more than 40% since the singer launched her Music, Fashion, Film tour last month. If you want to avoid spoilers, there's only one thing you can do, according to Snapes: "You have to not look at TikTok."If you want to be surprised, you have to protect yourself from absorbing any of that culture."Image source, Getty Images for AEGImage caption, Have you ever tried this one? Sabrina Carpenter had a number of special reveals for each show on her Short n' Sweet tourPhoebe Bridgers is taking things one step further to make sure fans are surprised at her shows - she's banning phones altogether.Those attending are required to lock their phones and any recording devices in a special pouch when they enter the venue to see the US singer. Anyone found breaking the rules will be escorted out. McAdam wouldn't support a ban on phones, saying recording at gigs is "part of the experience" for a lot of fans.But Collins says she's "not totally against it".What she'd prefer is to see more spoiler warnings on videos so fans have the option to be surprised if they want.But even if you know the set list, the staging and the outfits, "you're still probably going to get to see moments of humanity and stuff that's unplanned," Snapes adds. "I went to the Edinburgh Eras show where Taylor Swift was really snotty and she had to blow her nose. That's not part of the script."You're always going to be surprised."Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: Spoilers: Is social media ruining gig surprises?

title: Russia hits second major bridge in Ukraine's capital Kyiv
description: A Russian strike has hit a second major bridge in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko has said, as Moscow ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in Ukr
body: A Russian strike has hit a second major bridge in Kyiv, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko has said, as Moscow ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in Ukraine's capital.The attack on Saturday morning injured two people, and damaged the road surface and overhead trolleybus wires on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge, Klitschko said, causing traffic jams.It comes after the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge was hit multiple times by Russian drones this week, with Klitschko warning that "the enemy is tearing Kyiv apart".Russia said its drones had hit the two bridges used to transfer Ukrainian troops and military cargo. Moscow again urged foreign citizens, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv. The two Kyiv bridges across the Dnipro River link the western and eastern parts of the capital and had not been hit before Thursday.The Russian strikes have severed road, rail and trolleybus links across the wide river. The ongoing drone threat means restrictions on other routes, bringing traffic jams to the city's roads for a second day - though Friday's gridlock has not been repeated to the same level.Many of the city's residents - which number about three million - rely on the metro to travel across the city every day. The fear is this new Russian tactic will result in sustained attacks which could effectively cut the city in two.Writing on Telegram on Saturday morning, Klitschko said "emergency services are on their way" after the Pivnichnyi Bridge was hit."Traffic on the bridge from the left to the right bank is currently blocked," he added.Earlier attacks on the Pivdennyi Bridge prompted Kyiv's defence council to hold a crisis meeting on Friday. Klitschko warned afterwards that the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities.Experts say Russian drones are unlikely to bring down the bridges - but repeated attacks will force their closure and risk weakening their structure, making them unusable. More powerful weapons could collapse the bridges, some of which are reported to be in poor condition after years carrying heavier traffic than they were designed for.It was reported that Ukrainian lawmakers discussed the state of Kyiv's bridges in a recent meeting, setting out contingency plans to use ferries or temporary pontoon bridges to keep the city connected in the event of any bridges being destroyed.Russian President Vladimir Putin has said Russia is acting in response to Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy facilities, despite the fact that it was Moscow that had first launched such attacks.After the Pivdennyi Bridge was attacked, passengers described how dust from a blast wave entered their carriage through the ventilation system.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Putin had decided that there were "no rules now" when attacking Ukraine. In an interview with the Financial Times, he said: "The Russians have failed to occupy us. So now they are carrying out massive attacks and mass killings."He added: "They want to destroy our bridges... our data centres, the internet, mobile networks, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, universities - everything. They want people to flee their cities."Putin on Thursday insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries and its ships in the Black Sea."Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," Putin said after a wide-ranging speech at the Valdai foreign policy forum.The Kremlin leader admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helps the Kremlin finance the war.Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since Putin launched a full-scale invasion in February 2022.

schema.headline: Russia hits second major bridge in Ukraine's capital Kyiv

title: Republic of Ireland v Israel: News conference ends amid accusations
description: For more than 11 minutes of Saturday's pre-match news conference, Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson fielded questions centred on Sunday'
body: For more than 11 minutes of Saturday's pre-match news conference, Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson fielded questions centred on Sunday's Nations League Group B3 'home' game against Israel in Serbia.The Icelander revealed that Dara O'Shea - captain in place of the injured Nathan Collins - was not with the squad, as his wife was due to give birth. He may arrive back in Backa Topola prior to Sunday's 19:45 BST kick-off.Hallgrimsson also gave his thoughts on the strain of this four-game international window and reflected on Thursday's 2-2 draw against Austria.As the first section of the media conference, which is allowed to be broadcast live, was ending, the mood soured.One reporter tried to quiz Hallgrimsson on his thoughts about the incident on Wednesday when a co-pilot attacked a pilot on a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv, before passengers managed to overpower the attacker and successfully take control of the plane.The Republic of Ireland manager was also asked by another journalist about alleged racism by Irish players during last Sunday's 3-0 win over Israel in Hungary and refused to give up the microphone.Promptly, the news conference was brought to a close by Football Association of Ireland (FAI) head of communications Kieran Crowley after calling those allegations "completely untrue".The allegations of racism by an Irish player comes after it was confirmed the FAI is investigating reports of racist abuse directed towards Republic of Ireland striker Adam Idah by Israel fans in Debrecen.Minutes before the news conference was brought to an abrupt halt, Hallgrimsson insisted he would not be drawn on either matter and would not "get involved in that as others will process that"."It is a game with a lot of emotions attached," Hallgrimsson said."I haven't read anything and it's not something I want to get involved with. It goes to a process, both in our department and with Uefa. "Something was reported by both teams so I just hope we can focus on football and football will be the winner after this."I have not gone into details looking at this as I have enough to think about."Before last week's 'home' game for Israel in Hungary, goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu withdrew from the fixtures, saying "it would be wrong to participate" while a vote by players to play the games passed by a "significant majority", according to FAI chief executive David Courell.There were protests during the game against Austria in Dublin on Thursday, with tennis balls thrown on to the pitch and a protester briefly interrupting the game when he ran on to the turf, waving a Palestine flag.Hallgrimmson said under the circumstances, it will be a "a big win for this group and the association if we go through undamaged"."The most pleasing thing for me is to see the togetherness and how they stand up for each other. Whatever they have done, they have done it with respect to the situation, to each other and after this, this bond of brothers will be stronger than ever. All the obstacles this group will face in the future will be lesser than it is."When we look back, this camp will be a moment we grew the most and stepped up as leaders, supported each other and stuck together. The power of togetherness is stronger than individuals."

schema.headline: Republic of Ireland v Israel: News conference ends amid accusations

title: Bahrain GP in Malaysia 2026: Red Bull upgrade enlivens F1
description: Even Lewis Hamilton, starting from his equal best grid position of the year in second place, fears Max Verstappen will be tough to beat in Sunday's Ba
body: Even Lewis Hamilton, starting from his equal best grid position of the year in second place, fears Max Verstappen will be tough to beat in Sunday's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.Verstappen has dominated the weekend so far on Formula 1's return to the Sepang track for the first time since 2017.Hamilton joins him on the front row to revive memories of their no-holds-barred title battle five years ago.But at nearly 0.3 seconds slower in qualifying, and with the pace Verstappen has shown all weekend, Hamilton's mindset on Saturday was to "just try my best to hold on to him tomorrow".This was Verstappen's first pole position of the year - a remarkable statistic for someone who came within two points of winning a fifth world title last year after one of the all-time great fightbacks.Red Bull started the year off the pace - the car was on average more than 0.5secs a lap slower than Mercedes in the first half of the year - and for a time there were questions as to whether Verstappen would stick around for 2027.But after being courted by McLaren, Verstappen signed a two-year contract extension over the summer break, saying he believed in the Red Bull project and didn't mind putting in the work to turn things around. Verstappen arrived in Malaysia after a run of three consecutive podium finishes, and with Red Bull hoping to prove out an upgrade that had seen them finish less than 0.2secs off victory in Baku last Sunday.In the tropical heat of Malaysia, around the demanding long corners of this track with perhaps the roughest surface of the season, the upgrade - centred on a new floor - has more than proved its worth."It's been an incredible result for us," Verstappen said. "Looking at the season, how it started for us and the progression that we have made. At some tracks we were kind of close, but now I think this weekend it was very positive for us."We have been adding bits to the car and they have worked. It's simple as that. When they work, you gain lap time, you have a better overall balance in the car."So with tyres that are very sensitive to balance, that gives you also more lap time."And then on a track probably where it's all very hot and you want a, let's say, stable balance or connected balance, then that's very important. And that's what we have found a little bit more over the last weekends."Hamilton, for one, but also Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli, who under-performed slightly in qualifying because of a combination between an unusual tyre strategy and an error on an early run.The world championship leader's fourth place becomes third on the grid with Hadjar's penalty, and he can usually be relied upon to be a factor in the race.Antonelli's main focus will be his advantage over team-mate George Russell, who trails the Italian by 66 points and starts four places behind, his momentum from his Baku win stalled, and somewhat perplexed as to his and his team's lack of pace.At Mercedes, the bigger question is over the aerodynamic upgrade they brought to the car this weekend.Mercedes are lagging behind their rivals when it comes to developing their car this season, apparently at least in part because they front-loaded their spend early in the season.But this first big update since the Canadian Grand Prix in June has not yet proved the step they had expected.The question is whether that is to do with the parts themselves or the very specific conditions of this weekend, in the heat and on the rough track surface, which is putting the tyres through the mill, and massively limiting the useful laps teams can do in terms of set-up work.Antonelli said: "With this new package, obviously the window of the way the car operates is different. So, we're trying to understand in which window the car performance is best, in the high-speed corner and low-speed corners."Our high-speed performance has been very strong this weekend. We were very quick in the high-speed, but in the low-speed we lacked. So, we need to understand why and try to move on and improve."As for the race, Antonelli said: "Track position is going to be very important. Strategy is going to be really important."It's a race where we will attack. Because undercut (stopping first and gaining time on a rival on fresh tyres) is incredibly powerful."So whenever there's an opportunity, we should go for maybe an undercut and try to maximise our opportunity."Tomorrow might be two stops, three stops. We don't know. But the only thing we know is that it's going to be roasting hot out there."

schema.headline: Bahrain GP in Malaysia 2026: Red Bull upgrade enlivens F1

title: Why thousands of couples are choosing Scotland to say 'I do'
description: Chihon Ley Polanco, from Chile, and Ana-Maria Bucatari, from Moldova, came to Scotland to study, but the country quickly became the backdrop to their
body: Chihon Ley Polanco, from Chile, and Ana-Maria Bucatari, from Moldova, came to Scotland to study, but the country quickly became the backdrop to their love story.The couple first met in 2018 through a dance society at the University of Edinburgh, when Ana-Maria was on an Erasmus exchange and Chihon was completing his postgraduate studies.They they spent years as friends, and it was not until Ana-Maria returned to Edinburgh in 2024 that their relationship became something more. And their romance blossomed in the same place their friendship had years earlier."Everything happened again on the dance floor," Ana-Maria said.Just four months after getting engaged, the pair walked down the aisle on the Isle of Arran.The couple said they "fell in love" with the island at first sight, due to it having the "complete scenery of Scotland". "You feel that you're in a magical place", said Chihon. "It's very unique."The couple said Scotland felt like the natural choice."We're from two different continents," Chihon said. "Scotland is where we met and where we built our life together."

schema.headline: Why thousands of couples are choosing Scotland to say 'I do'

title: Why electric cars might be making some passengers feel sick
description: EV drivers love their cars, but some passengers feel sick - this could be whyImage source, Getty Images/Halfpoint ImagesByGrace DeanLola Baird has jus
body: EV drivers love their cars, but some passengers feel sick - this could be whyImage source, Getty Images/Halfpoint ImagesByGrace DeanLola Baird has just asked her boyfriend to pull over. Forty minutes into a journey and she's feeling "overwhelmed" by nausea - and can't stop herself throwing up on the ground next to his car.Lola, 24, from north London, had never experienced motion sickness until her boyfriend bought an electric vehicle (EV) two years ago. Ever since, she's been feeling "very nauseous" when he takes her on long car journeys.It's become so severe she's even asked him to change his car.Lola isn't alone. Other people told BBC News that they or their children notice feeling more car sick when sitting as a passenger in an electric vehicle. But at the same time, many EV drivers say it's not been a concern.So what could explain these reports of motion sickness?Dr Irene Di Giulio, senior lecturer in anatomy and biomechanics at King's College London whose research includes motion sickness, says research so far suggests some people experience more severe motion sickness in electric vehicles than in non-electric vehicles.It's something Dr Nicholas Hac, a neurologist at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago who specialises in dizziness and vertigo, has also heard from some of his patients. "They just notice that they're much more likely or prone to be motion sick" in electric vehicles, he says."I've heard about it many, many, many times," he adds, saying about two patients a month specifically reference feeling motion sick in electric vehicles.Image source, Lola BairdImage caption, Lola Baird noticed that she felt sick in electric vehicle taxis as well as her boyfriend's car. "I started to put two and two together," she saysBut research into any possible link is still in its early stages, and some academics say there isn't sufficient evidence to say anything definitive.Dr Bill Yates, who has researched motion sickness at the University of Pittsburgh, says the body of research is "pretty sketchy at this point"."There's some anecdotal information, but not a lot of really serious, extensive studies done yet," he says.'Wonderful to drive... but my daughter gets unwell'When Mark Quigg was looking at options for a new car last year, an electric vehicle seemed like the best choice because of the lower running costs. Mark, 45, from Lincolnshire, says his shiny new electric vehicle has been "wonderful" to drive - but he quickly noticed that his nine-year-old daughter's motion sickness got much worse in it.She only used to get motion sick on their 600-mile drives to France during the school holidays, but now he says even the 30-minute trip to the nearest city makes his daughter feel unwell.On one recent journey, he says his daughter even threw up, which had never happened before.Image source, Mark QuiggImage caption, Mark Quigg says electric cars are a "lovely driving experience for me, personally, because they are a lot quieter"Motion sickness doesn't affect all EV passengers - many owners got in touch with BBC News to say they and their relatives don't get sick in electric vehicles. Others said they felt less sick in EVs compared with traditional combustion engine cars.Vicky Edmonds, the CEO of EVA England, an association for electric vehicle drivers, says motion sickness isn't a concern among her members. "This has never come up as an issue," she says.But Chinese electric vehicle maker XPeng, which has showrooms across the UK, has previously publicly addressed the issue, external, telling people who've noticed a link between electric vehicles and travel sickness that "it's a fair question, and it's not your imagination". It's caused by "side effects of how electric cars are engineered," it adds.What could cause it?Motion sickness is caused by "a mismatch in sensory cues," Hac says. Our bodies rely on three main sensory inputs to show that we're moving, which come from what we see, what our inner ear's balance system perceives, and what fibres in our body sense, he says. When one of these is in conflict with the others - like if you're looking at your phone so you don't see visual signs of movement out of the window - that can cause motion sickness.Research suggests several reasons why it may be more severe in electric vehicles.Humans have adapted to associate sound with movement in vehicles, experts explain. Because electric vehicles don't have the auditory cues and vibrations from the engine that we're used to, which indicate when the car is accelerating, this could trigger motion sickness, Di Giulio says.Another reason is regenerative braking, the process whereby when drivers release the accelerator, the motor starts acting as a generator. This creates resistance that slows the car down and also produces electricity that can be stored in the battery. The accelerator needs to be released gently, or it can lead to harsh deceleration."It forces the person to perhaps feel like they're rocking back and forth for that brief moment when the speed of the car suddenly changes," says Hac.This is something Carolyn Le, 24, from California, has noticed. She gets "horrendous" motion sickness when her friend drives her in his electric vehicle in busy cities, she says. The regenerative braking means it "constantly feels like the car is stopping all the time".Image source, Carolyn LeImage caption, "It's actually horrendous," says Carolyn Le, who blames regenerative braking for her motion sicknessElectric vehicles can also accelerate and decelerate much more quickly than conventional combustion cars, which Di Giulio says can cause motion sickness.Edmonds, of EVA England, says developments in electric vehicle design have made them better at moderating the acceleration so they don't gain speed as rapidly.She adds that the association thinks motion sickness in an electric vehicle is caused by "other factors" like the motorist's driving style rather than the vehicle itself. Some features of electric cars may feel unfamiliar to drivers at first, adds Mike Hawes, head of the Society of Motor Manufacturers.He says EVs can offer a different driving experience. "However, drivers typically adjust quickly to these characteristics, and many models also allow regenerative braking to be tailored to individual preferences."Some people are also just more prone to motion sickness, and genetics have the biggest influence on this, according to Hac, and experts say women and children are more susceptible.Motion sickness typically peaks between the ages of eight and 10, after which it decreases through more exposure, says Prof John Golding, who has researched the subject at the University of Westminster, the Royal Navy and the RAF.Hold your head still and open the windowAs their popularity increases, avoiding electric vehicles can be a challenge - the number of new zero-emission cars registered in the UK rose by 40.5% in April to June 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, latest Department for Transport figures show. , externalAt the end of June 2026, 5.8% of all licensed cars on UK roads were zero-emission vehicles, the data shows. The sale of new purely petrol or diesel cars is set to be banned from 2030.Lucinda Harrison, 24, from London says she often books taxis that turn out to be electric vehicles, and has to endure the trip feeling nauseous, sweaty and clammy.The thought of travelling in an EV fills her with dread, she says. Even just a five-minute lift from a colleague to a Tube station recently was enough to make her feel "horrific".Academics say there are several steps passengers can take to reduce feelings of motion sickness.Look out of the front window and don't look at your phone or read a bookSit in the front passenger seat rather than in the back, if possible. If you do have to sit in the back, opt for the middle seat so you can still see out the front windowKeep your head still by holding it against the headrestRecline your seatRegulate your breathingOpen the window to let in fresh airTake travel sickness tablets if needed, though these can cause drowsinessBefore a long journey, make sure you're hydrated, have slept well and have eaten non-greasy foodExperts also say we can become desensitised to motion sickness through prolonged exposure. The more journeys you take in electric vehicles, the less likely you are to become motion sick as your body adjusts, Golding says.Image source, Getty Images/Cyndi MonaghanImage caption, Looking out the window can ease motion sickness, which children and women may be more prone to experiencing as passengersThere are also things carmakers can do to alleviate motion sickness in electric vehicles, says Prof Cyriel Diels, professor of mobility design at the Royal College of Art. These include having software that smooths out rapid acceleration, adding sound systems and subtle seat vibrations to signal to passengers that the car is moving, and offering adaptive regenerative braking that reduces sudden deceleration.In some EVs, regenerative braking can also often be turned off.Matt Adams from BEAMA, which represents UK manufacturers of electric vehicle charge points, says he's confident that "if future research identifies the reason for car sickness that vehicle manufacturers can respond and improve accordingly".But for Lola, she just wants her boyfriend to trade in his car. She says that day can't come soon enough.Get in touchAre you an EV driver or have been a passenger in an EV? Have you experienced nausea due to motion sickness? Tell us your story.

schema.headline: Why electric cars might be making some passengers feel sick

title: Newcastle friends embark on 20-year board game battle
description: Image source, War With A MateImage caption, James Purcell and Andy Taeger will officially start Campaign for North Africa on 30 OctoberByEvie LakeNort
body: Image source, War With A MateImage caption, James Purcell and Andy Taeger will officially start Campaign for North Africa on 30 OctoberByEvie LakeNorth East and CumbriaTwo friends from Newcastle have set themselves the challenge of completing a board game which has never officially been completed. They expect it will take 20 years as they battle to fit it around their everyday lives - but while games can often put friendships to the test, the pair are determined to see it through, no matter how different life will look.What would you be willing to commit 1,500 hours of your life doing?Playing a game about a week during World War Two in North Africa might not be top of your list - but James Purcell, 29, and Andy Taeger, 30, decided to do just that.The pair met about a decade ago at a house party and became fast friends after duetting to a James Blunt song.They have spent every week since playing Dungeons and Dragons together."One day we were playing and this friend just mentioned off-handedly that there was a game that supposedly had never been finished and takes up to 1,500 hours," Purcell says."We had a bit of a laugh about it, thought nothing of it, and then a few weeks later we were at the pub and one of us said 'have you been thinking about that board game a lot?'"They spent the next few hours in the pub discussing it and left committed to playing Campaign for North Africa in its entirety.18-month drawThat was in October 2024. And for Purcell and Taeger, there's no going back.The strategic board wargame was released in 1978 and simulates the entire North African campaign of World War Two. Purcell says there has been no evidenced play of the full game and theirs would be the first occasion."The game was never fully playtested by the designers either," he adds.Now two years on from their original commitment, the pair have managed a six-turn practice run to get to grips with the rules before jumping into the full game, which is 111 turns.Every turn simulates a real week during World War Two in North Africa. Purcell is playing as the Axis forces - Germany, Italy, Japan - while Taeger is playing as the Commonwealth.While 10 players are suggested, they are making do with just two.Through spreadsheets they have to keep track of things like ammunition, food, fuel, water, even down to the rate at which water evaporates depending on the heat.Image source, War With A MateImage caption, A practice run took more than a year to completeThe practice ended in a draw and took 18 months to complete alongside their jobs and everyday lives.Purcell works in mental health services while Taeger is a software developer."It feels sometimes like a job as well, we're filling out spreadsheets more so than playing a game, so a lot of the time it doesn't feel like fun, it feels like admin," Purcell says.To hold themselves accountable, they set up a podcast, War With A Mate, which has already had more than 90 episodes.And it has a good following already, with Purcell joking it is nice not having to bribe his friends and family to listen along.Finding common groundBut board games are known to get tense, even more so if you are at war with one another, and the friends are mindful of that."We're trying to keep it fairly chill, but sometimes it'll come down to a single dice roll and someone gets unlucky and there has been a bit of, not quite throwing pieces around because the board's too big, but there have been moments of frustration and tension," Taeger says.Purcell adds: "I've had a few hissy fits, just with the rules being so complicated."I've been a bit annoyed when we've been so far in and I've realised I've done something wrong and had to make new plans based on that."Because to finish a single turn, it takes us months at a time."But their podcast has a segment called Common Ground which forces the pair to try and agree on something from the episode, no matter how ridiculous.They are hopeful it will stop them fighting.'20-year void'The friends are now gearing up to starting their official Campaign for North Africa on 30 October, which will coincide with the podcast's 100th episode."I think when we start the full game, it'll be exciting," Purcell says."And then from there we've got the sort of void of 20 plus years that it'll take to finish the game."So I'm kind of worried that the excitement might wear off and then we're just locked into this thing for two decades."War With A Mate already has listeners from around the globe, many of whom are happy they get to experience the game without having to do hundreds of hours of legwork."I think at certain times it'll be our biggest regret starting it and sometimes it'll be some real highs," Taeger says."But I think it'll be part people listening along to our deteriorating mental state."It is certain the pair's lives will look different after 20 years, when they hope to have completed the game.Purcell says: "It's sort of weird knowing that we'll be 20 years older."We can have any sort of different living circumstance, careers, so it's strange that this game is going to be a constant through that and it already has for two years."So it'll be interesting to see how it maps across."Follow BBC Newcastle on X, external, Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Newcastle on BBC Sounds.Get in touchDo you have a story suggestion for BBC Tyne?

title: Widdecombe suspect charged with planning acts of terror against Farage
description: The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe has also been charged with preparing acts of terror including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.Counte
body: The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe has also been charged with preparing acts of terror including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.Counter terror police said Joshua Kerry, 28, was charged on Friday with one count of preparation of terrorist acts.The charge relates to activity which is alleged to have taken place between May 2024 and July 2026. Kerry was charged in July with the murder of 78-year-old Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman.Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said she knew the fresh charge would be "extremely concerning" and her "profound sympathies" were with Farage and his family."Let no one make any mistake: an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all."This case raises serious questions about the security of those in public life. We must use this as an opportunity to reset. Once parliament returns, I will update on our work to strengthen protections for those who choose to serve."The BBC contacted Reform UK for comment and a party source said: "This is exactly why Nigel needed £5m to protect his security for life."Farage is currently facing a parliamentary standards watchdog probe into a £5m gift from a billionaire donor before he returned as an MP in 2024. The Reform leader has previously said the money was for his personal security.Deputy leader of Reform UK, Richard Tice, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the murder of Ann Widdecombe had made everyone take security more seriously."What's particularly upsetting for those of us in and around him [Farage] is sometimes he's not been believed, not been listened to."Tice added that he personally had security arrangements in place and his habits had changed which was a "consequence of the world we live in" arguing the "online world has clearly hindered this whole process".Asked if Reform had done enough to dial the temperature down and whether comments from politicians added to public anger, Tice said "the passions that flow through democratic debate should be completely separate to the way that people respond "It's the nature of democracy... it's part of the joy of it is that there will be robust debate but at the end of it one should be able to shake hands." Counter Terrorism Policing Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans said the charge on Friday was the result of a "hugely intensive and complex investigation". "This investigation has been led by a dedicated team of detectives, analysts, and forensic experts, working on multiple lines of enquiry, which has resulted in this very serious charge," she added.Kerry, from Rotherham, is due to appear in court over the terror charge on Wednesday, police said.Frank Ferguson of the Crown Prosecution Service's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division said prosecutors "worked closely" with police to bring the charge and would continue to work alongside them as the investigation continued.Widdecombe was found dead on Thursday 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries.She served as Conservative MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.Following her departure from the Commons, Widdecombe appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing and would later become a Reform UK spokeswoman.

title: Protesters across Spain demand action over housing crisis
description: Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants after the government failed to get emergenc
body: Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants after the government failed to get emergency housing legislation through parliament on Friday.About 50 planned marches are taking place on Saturday in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona ."There is a lot of anger in the streets," said a spokesperson for the Valencia Tenants' Union, where a demonstration has already started. Clashes have taken place between some protesters and police in the city.The measures put forward by Pedro Sánchez's leftist coalition government on Friday followed public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home last month after she was unable to afford a sharp rent increase.Her eviction triggered nationwide protests across Spain with protesters demanding lower rents, an end to evictions, and a ban on investment funds - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property.Sanchez's defeat in Congress on Friday heightens speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer. His coalition government, made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, does not command a majority in parliament.The legislation put forward in Congress on Friday was divided into two separate decrees.The first decree included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by  so-called "vulture funds".The second decree included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Tenants' Union.MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166.Prior to the vote, the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country.However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure.Sánchez's ruling coalition hurriedly drew up the decree laws in an effort to defuse the housing protests that were sparked when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted in September.The social backlash led to the company that owns Abascal's flat, Urbagestión, negotiating her return to the flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued.

schema.headline: Protesters across Spain demand action over housing crisis

title: Suppliers pile pressure on government over energy bills
description: The government should take immediate action to help those struggling with energy bills this winter, the suppliers' trade body has said.Energy UK said
body: The government should take immediate action to help those struggling with energy bills this winter, the suppliers' trade body has said.Energy UK said domestic gas prices, which rose on Thursday, and forecasts of steep rises in January meant inaction would lead to a longer-term, more costly and deeper crisis.Figures revealed by the BBC earlier this week showed forecasters predicting a 16% rise in domestic energy prices in the new year for 20 million households on variable tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the government was considering any measure that took the pressure off.Households in England, Scotland and Wales on variable energy tariffs set by Ofgem's price cap, which puts a maximum price on each unit of gas and electricity, were hit with a 4% price increase at the start of October.That is the equivalent of about £60 per year - or £5 per month - taking an annual bill to £1,723 for the typical household using both electricity and gas and paying by direct debit if this level was sustained for a year.But forecasts show a far greater increase is possible for bills in January. Consultancy Cornwall Insight said its latest forecast suggested the same typical annual bill would rise to £1,999.On Thursday, the boss of supplier EDF Energy, Simone Rossi, warned that the UK was "walking into a second energy crisis" and Vyas said that action was needed before bills jumped again."Last-minute emergency interventions run the risk of being badly targeted and costing us all more," she said.Energy UK is calling for government measures including:targeted support over and above the £150 Warm Home Discount, given to people on benefits, which would eventually lead to the introduction of a discounted social tariffa debt relief scheme for the most severely affected households as part of a strategy that will also help prevent debt build-up among new tenants and homeownersremoving more levies from electricity bills and shifting them to taxation, as part of a wider move to electrificationAdam Scorer, chief executive of charity National Energy, which campaigns against fuel poverty, told BBC Breakfast he agreed with what Energy UK's analysis. "[The increase in debt is] not more people getting into debt, that's more poor people getting into more serious levels of debt." He added: "Until you do something about that, there's no way forward, there's no breathing space, there's no future for households who can't see their way beyond debt."At the Labour Party conference last week, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC that he would not call Rossi's crisis warning an overstatement, adding that the cost of home energy, as well as petrol and diesel, was "very difficult indeed"."We're looking at any measure that can give people breathing space, that can take the pressure off," he said.

schema.headline: Suppliers pile pressure on government over energy bills

title: You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to save it
description: Figure caption, How much is in your savings account?ByCost of living correspondentIf buying your own home is the finishing line, then saving up the mo
body: Figure caption, How much is in your savings account?ByCost of living correspondentIf buying your own home is the finishing line, then saving up the money to get there is a marathon.The "Your First Home" scheme, announced on Saturday, aims to help first-time buyers in England get on the housing ladder with a small deposit.Currently a 5% deposit on the average UK house price of £272,000 plus moving costs and legal fees - will set you back about £16,850, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.That's daunting, but here are four ways that experts say you can at least make a start on saving for a deposit.1. Make saving like a billDepositing an amount you can afford into a regular savers account the day after you are paid is a good way to start, suggests Anna Bowes, savings expert at financial advisers The Private Office."It becomes like another bill, but one that you can benefit from in the future," she says.The type of account that's suitable depends on your circumstances.Some of the ones that pay the highest interest  are only accessible if you hold a current account with the provider, she says.Other considerations are whether you can lock the money away for longer, to receive a better savings rate.If you don't have a buffer of other savings, then experts say an easy access account gives you the chance to dip into the money to pay an unexpected bill.2. You could get £1,000 a year You can save up to £4,000 a year in a Lifetime Individual Savings Account (LISA) and the government guarantees a 25% bonus. So, if you put the full amount in then the government will add £1,000 a year. But there is a catch, that has left some people out of pocket. Money saved in a LISA can only be used to buy a first home up to the value of £450,000 - a threshold that has not changed since 2017. The only other time you can withdraw the money is after the age of 60 or in the exceptional case that you are terminally ill with less than 12 months to live.Withdrawal under any other circumstances means you get hit with a penalty - so you could get back less than you put in.Ministers are planning to replace the LISA with a new First Time Buyer ISA, but there are no clear details yet about how it will work.3. Start earlyThe earlier you start saving the more you can build up thanks to the magic of compound interest. In short, interest is added on a larger and larger pot as time goes by.Bowes says that saving £50 a month from the age of 20 would give you about £41,000 in 30 years' time when you hit 50, assuming interest of 5% is paid a year.Start 10 years later, and you'd need to save more than double - £101 a month - to have the same amount at the age of 50.Investing in stocks and shares is another option, but the value of investments can go down as well as up.4. Save lessAn increasing number of lenders are offering mortgage deals with little or no deposit required.David Hollingworth, from L&C, points to mortgages that have deposits starting from £5,000 and allow people to borrow up to 98% or 99% of the property purchase price.They might not always be the best option, and not everyone will be eligible.And, of course, some first-time buyers turn to their parents for help. Again that's not available to all, but a survey by the Nationwide Building Society suggests that more than half of parents who charge their adult children rent are putting some or all of the money towards helping their child save to buy their own home.Get in touchAre you trying to get on to the property ladder? Share your experience. Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: You need £17,000 for a first home - here's how to save it
